5. Further case of the original plaintiff is that he settled the suit land for one year from Baishakh 1344 B.S. to one Jayanta Singha who executed a kabuliyat dated 1st Bhadra 1344 B.S. and after expiry of one year Jayanta Singha made over possession to the original plaintiff on 1st Baishakh 1345 B.S. Subsequently, one Mrs. Rosemary Keymer and her husband Mr. W. C. Keymer took lease of the western part of the suit land from the original plaintiff for 10 years by registered lease deed dated 19.12.1944 and they having possessed the said land for 2 years surrendered possession to the original plaintiff. 

 9. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Amu Singha in fate right who took settlement from the original plaintiff by executing kabuliyat dated Ashar 1344 B.S. While Amu Singha was living therein, he died leaving his son Krishna Singha, who died unmarried leaving his only nephew (sister's son) defendant No.2 as his only heir. Accordingly, defendant No.2 held and possessed the suit land. During settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Krishna Singha noting the name of the original plaintiff as landlord. The plaintiff in collusion with the Objection Officer changed the record-of—right in his name. Defendant No.2 then filed appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was allowed on contest on 09.09.1961. The further case of defendant No.1 is that defendant No.2 was possessing the suit land partly as homestead and partly as chara bari (abandoned homestead) and then he transferred part of the suit land as noted in schedule II of the written statement by kabala dated 07.08.1965 to defendant No.1 and delivered possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing part of the suit land purchased by him as stated above by constructing but and planting trees. The plaintiff is cunning and he took defendant No.2 in his confidence with high hopes that he would buy the land at a high price. Defendant No.2 having decided to sell part of the suit land to defendant No.1 began to kill time and refused presentation of kabala for registration and defendant No.1 then presented the kabala dated 07.08.1965 for registration before the Sub-registrar. Defendant No.2 did not appear at the instance of the plaintiff. So defendant No.1 had to file appeal before the District Registrar and the kabala was registered on contest on 02.02.1966. The plaintiff and defendant No.2 are in collusion and under influence of the plaintiff, defendant No.2 is remaining silent. 

 26. In the facts of the instant case discussed above, we find that the High Court Division has reversed the concurrent finding of facts of the Courts below without specifically identifying any evidence which was misread or not considered by the trial Court or the appellate Court. The reference to non-consideration of the deed in favour of Irfan Ali Chowdhury dating to 1927 is of little consequence in view of the fact that admittedly the defendants' predecessors were the tenants in possession of the suit land from the original owners, having jote right by way of registered kabuliyat, and the record of rights was in their names as tenants. Irfan Ali Chowdhury purchased the land with the defendants' predecessor in possession as tenant. The finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court is that the plaintiffs could not prove that Irfan Ali Chowdhury ever went into possession of the suit land.
